comments.text:
To all the people complaining about the lack of a generational uplift..  it's just a name. Do you care what your GPU is called? It's about price and performance. 

Prices this generation are up all around. I went from a 6800XT to a 7900XT and can confirm, the 7900XT is the RDNA3 equivalent of the 6800XT.

Yeah the 7900XT is much more expensive than the 6800XT was..  but keep in mind prices are being driven up massively by the demand for AI. The chips used for AI share production capacity with gaming GPUs, while being like 10x more profitable and a severe lack of production capacity (hence the building of multiple new chip fabs), and they have to answer to shareholders. 

Gaming GPUs are basically a charity at this point. Production of both Ada and RDNA3 are low, with prices high and dropping very slowly. Because in the end they will be bought anyway, and if not, then prices can be dropped later. You can expect the next generation to be even more expensive. Both nvidia and AMD have been trying to mask this by naming their GPUs a tier higher than what they really are and focusing on software solutions like upscaling and frame gen in an attempt to keep PC gaming more affordable.

That is what makes this card special! A modern RDNA3 GPU with 6800XT performance, 16GB VRAM on a 256-bit bus, and they actually went for the $499 sweet spot. This is easily the best value 1440P card of this entire GPU generation. AMD likely did this to grab some market share. 6800XT stock is nearly dried up, it's getting more difficult to find by the day and will disappear soon.

The target audience are not RDNA2 owners, but people on RDNA/Turing and older generation cards looking for a good value upgrade with enough VRAM. And the 7800XT delivers, no matter what it's called. Anyone with an RDNA/Turing GPU or older will be eyeing this card and it's already sold out in many places, with more stock coming next week.

comments.text:
GPUs aren't rocket science their value is in how much performance they offer to their price and how many dies you can get per wafer essentially. 

This is all VERY rough on the edges where I don't have all the information but as a baseline in the UK the 6800XT release price was £599, the 6800XT in rasterisation based games is roughly 15% better on average I'd have to look at more games for a more complete and accurate figure so we'll start with very simple math by taking 15% from the 6800XT launch price, that brings the value down to £509.15, we then factor in that the 7800XT SHOULD be cheaper to produce as a whole because of the smaller 5nm lithography compared to the 68XTs 7nm which means AMD get more dies\chiplets per wafer, 78XT total die size is 346mm while 6800XT is 520mm. We can only estimate how many dies AMD get per wafer but to keep things simple let's say AMD get 100 dies for the 6800XT @ 520mm that means for the 78XT you'd theoretically get about 33% more dies from the same size wafer, yields not withstanding so let's say that AMD could reduce the price another 10% there due to them being able to get another 33 dies out of that same size wafer on the smaller 5nm node. That reduces the price to £458.23. From what I know there is also no GDDR shortages so chances are AMD are getting a discount there from buying in bulk, no idea what that could possibly be but let's be modest and say 4% per 1000 pieces  so the per unit 78XT price is then £439.90. Standard coolers aren't expensive to produce so I'll include production and design costs in that £439.90. We then need to consider that the 7800XT has about 16% fewer shaders, HALF the amount of L3 cache (64BM vs 128MB), around 15% fewer texture units and again about 16% fewer ROPs. All of these factors also make the card significantly cheaper and easier to produce - failed 7900XT/XTX dies will become 7800XT dies, for instance. Last but not least AFAIK the chiplet design itself is also meant to be significantly cheaper to make than a standard monolithic design. This is how I comfortably arrive at an RRP of in and around the £400 mark for a reference model it's just marketing wanting to have their cake and eat it too.

This is me basing things on a little more than just conjecture, I have done work for, and still do some work for, certain organisations in the IT arena so there is some inside knowledge here. The people that really have it hard are the AIBs both AMD and nvidia are guilty of charging WAY more than they need to AIBs making the profit margins AIBs get very minimal indeed and in the case of when you see a GPU on sale chances are that AIB is actually losing money on each unit sold. At best this is AMD price gouging for a newly released product (which is fine, happens with everything) and at worst (and more likely) AMD slapping the "XT" badge on something with the specification of what would otherwise be a non-XT model. I also say "more likely" because AMD themselves have tried saying the 7800XT is a "true 6800 successor". That being the case, just go and buy a used 6800 instead they can be had for £380 or less. The 7800 "XT" is a £400 7800. Watch this space for a 7800XTX model for £550-600.

If you consider that there's been higher than normal inflation in the last three years, and if you also consider what the launch MSRP pricing was for the 6800 XT and the 6700 XT, then the 7800 XT is actually providing a rather significant improvement in value per dollar. 

500 USD today is equivalent to around 440 USD two and a half years ago, when the 6700 XT first launched at 480 USD. The 6700 XT was probably originally planned to launch at closer to 440 USD, and maybe even less, but the 7800 XT is still about 43% faster, with 33% more Vram, more memory bandwidth, and various other new features and improvements which come with the new architecture as well, so the 7800 XT would still be a decent improvement in value over the 6700 XT, even if it had launched with an MSRP closer to 400 USD in early 2021. 

Against the 6800 XT's launch MSRP of 650 USD, the 7800 XT offers about a 50% improvement in value per dollar, if you properly account for inflation.

500 USD today is also equivalent to about 418 USD back in 2019, when the 5700 XT launched at 400 USD, and was considered a great value at that price. The 7800 XT is roughly 80-90% faster than the 5700 XT, but also has double the Vram capacity.

comments.text: I believe the 6800 is AMDs greatest card in a LONG time, actually since the R9 290.  It's EASILY the smartest buy.  I get 16,800 with an overclock in TimeSpy graphics with a dirty old 2600k, whereas my 6950xt at stock is a smidge under 19,000.  One cards RRP is $580, the other is $1100.  Before buying any Navi 2 card I looked at ALL the reviews and  benchmarks.  It stood out to me that in a hell of a lot of games, you might increase ROP and CU count by 20% (6800 vs 6800XT), but you certainly do not get equal scaling to FPS.  This happenes when there are bottlenecks elwhere in the system.  Sure, some great titles like Doom might give linear scaling from the 6800 to 6800XT to 6900XT to 6950XT, but actually, more often than not, the scaling is not linear, and the increase of 33% more CU might only give 15% more performance.  You can really never be sure if you are running into a memory bandwidth limitation, or a ROP or compute limitation.  However, clock speed is the fix all for bo matter where in the GPU core the limitation is, and with Navi2 cards, you aren't ever gaming at the maximum allowed frequency.  If you WERE gaming at the maximum core frequency, you would almost certainly get a nice performance uplift (unless it's a memory limitation).  To get that frequency up, you don't overclock, that's entirely pointless, you won't have power available to use the higher frequency of an overclock, that's the entire issue.  You want to raise the power limit.  If the 6800 and the 6900XT had the same power limit, many, many games, especially DX11 games would be no where near the massive 33% performance difference increase in FPS.    Look at the 7800XT vs the 7900GRE.  Both have a 260w power limit, both perform almost exactly identically.  1 has 3840 shaders (like a 6800) the other has 5120 shaders (like a 6950XT).  AND the 7900GRE has twice the L0 per workgroup processor and twice the L1 per array 50% more L2.  That HUGE amount of difference is wasted in the 7900GRE, because it doesn't have the power budget to use the shaders even if a game engine could make efficient use of them vs the 7800XT.  But I bet COD MW2 is way faster on the GRE.  Anyway I'm not saying that the 3840SE will always be as fast as 5120SE, or even most of the time, but I am saying that if you are actually savvy with your money and REALLY want the best deal, personally I would like a 7900GRE and run 360 watts through it and get it close to a 7900XTX, although it won't keep up at higher resolutions such as 4K for 2 reasons: 1) the memory bus is 50% wider on the 7900XTX which matters for higher resolutions where you are moving around more data and 2) the 7900XTX also has 50% more cache which again, same as memory (because it IS memory) more needed for higher resolutions.  But, at 1080P where you are getting more similar cache hits to L3 on both cards, man you can get performance super close, and the price difference is significant.  Alternatively to the 7900GRE, grab the 6800 if you are on a strict budget.  I got an ex-mining 6800 over 12 months ago for $450AUD (like $300USD?), and it rips

comments.text: @JustSomeDude31  you can put whatever you want on a board. A clamshell or partial clamshell needs completely new board anyway. The die in 4070 (and 4070ti) has a 6 channel memory controller. Nvidia uses 2GB Micron GDDR6X memory ICs in their higher end cards. That means 12GB cards have one 2GB memory IC per channel. To get 16GB you would have to add a 2GB memory IC to 2 of the 6 memory channels in a partial clamshell configuration. The problem is that the last 4GB of memory would only have 1/3 of the bandwidth the first 12GB has.

comments.text:
The 6700 XT is the 7800 XT's predecessor, don't be ridiculous. 

The 7800 XT naming is dumb. It's a 6700 XT successor, because it's using a mid-sized GPU, and its launching at a similar MSRP that the 6700 XT launched at. 500 USD today is equivalent to around 440 USD two and a half years ago, when the 6700 XT first launched at 480 USD, and the 7800 XT is about 43% faster than the 6700 XT.

It's nothing new for previous gen graphics cards to be heavily discounted in price before many of the next gen cards replace them, and for them to have equal or better performance per dollar at those prices, yet many people are arguing things like "the 7800 XT offers little to no improvement in value per dollar over the previous generation", as if AMD is supposed to give us a major improvement in value per dollar over CURRENT pricing for the already heavily discounted 6800 XT (and other various heavily discounted 6000 series cards). 

Do you need to like the price of the 7800 XT? No. It sucks that average incomes haven't kept pace with inflation, and you could argue that AMD does share some degree of blame for that, though certainly not most of the blame. 

If 500 is still too expensive for you, then that sucks, because the 7700 XT is not worth considering at current pricing (even though it is fairly competitive against Nvidia alternatives). The 6700 XT is currently a potentially very good option at 330 USD, but stock will probably mostly run out long before the next generation comes out, and the 7700 XT is simply too close in manufacturing cost to the 7800 XT for AMD to ever want to give us a genuinely good deal on them. AMD definitely left a big gap between the 7600 (which is itself still over-priced at most retailers), and the 7800 XT, basically forcing people to buy previous gen, or used cards, if they want a good value lower-mid-range or upper-low-end graphics card, and Nvidia has also basically done the same thing, by offering poor value for everything other than the RTX 4070 (and the 4090 is arguably a good value as well, at least as far as ultra high-end cards go, but it's simply not going to be worth buying for the vast majority of gamers).

comments.text:
The 7800 XT naming is dumb. It's a 6700 XT successor, because it's using a mid-sized GPU, and its launching at a similar MSRP that the 6700 XT launched at. 500 USD today is equivalent to around 440 USD two and a half years ago, when the 6700 XT first launched at 480 USD, and the 7800 XT is about 43% faster than the 6700 XT.

It's nothing new for previous gen graphics cards to be heavily discounted in price before many of the next gen cards replace them, and for them to have equal or better performance per dollar at those prices, yet many people are arguing things like "the 7800 XT offers little to no improvement in value per dollar over the previous generation", as if AMD is supposed to give us a major improvement in value per dollar over CURRENT pricing for the already heavily discounted 6800 XT (and other various heavily discounted 6000 series cards). 

Do you need to like the price of the 7800 XT? No. It sucks that average incomes haven't kept pace with inflation, and you could argue that AMD does share some degree of blame for that, though certainly not most of the blame. 

If 500 is still too expensive for you, then that sucks, because the 7700 XT is not worth considering at current pricing (even though it is fairly competitive against Nvidia alternatives). The 6700 XT is currently a potentially very good option at 330 USD, but stock will probably mostly run out long before the next generation comes out, and the 7700 XT is simply too close in manufacturing cost to the 7800 XT for AMD to ever want to give us a genuinely good deal on them. AMD definitely left a big gap between the 7600 (which is itself still over-priced at most retailers), and the 7800 XT, basically forcing people to buy previous gen, or used cards, if they want a good value lower-mid-range or upper-low-end graphics card, and Nvidia has also basically done the same thing, by offering poor value for everything other than the RTX 4070 (and the 4090 is arguably a good value as well, at least as far as ultra high-end cards go, but it's simply not going to be worth buying for the vast majority of gamers).

Objectively speaking, the 7800XT is a replacement to the 5700XT same memory bus, similar silicon size(including the much cheaper MCDs) just on a new node for the compute die which allows for more compute units.
And the price is somewhat reasonable after 4 years with the $399 MSRP of the 5700xt being around $465 in today's money.
My problem, much like the entire Nvidia lineup, is the name.
Just call the card what it is, its an X700 class card(on the small side of 70/700 class but its over 330mm so not quite 60 class, as opposed to the 5700xt which was squarely in 60/600 class at ~250mm)
Just because Nvidia is calling their 70/700 class card a 4080 and pricing it as a Titan, doesnt mean we should ignore the improperly named AMD lineup just because they're priced somewhat reasonably

Intel is doing it right, a 400mm advanced node die, the same size as the 4080, same memory bus as the 4080, same memory capacity as the 4080, just a slightly older node, and slower memory modules.
Calling it A770 and pricing it where 70/700 class cards used to be priced, part of that is that they want to gain market share and their drivers are crap, but hey, fairly priced is fairly priced.

comments.text:
That's normal with Ampere. It doesn't scale well downwards because Nvidia switched to a dual render core layout where one core can do INT or FP and the other can only do FP. But that "or" is significant. As soon as there are ANY INT instructions in the pipeline it can't do any FP instructions. The problem is that the INT-to-FP ratio changes between resolution. The higher the resolution the more the ratio skews towards FP. This was covered in great detail by HUB when Ampere launched. RDNA2 is the exact opposite. Because of it's large caches it scales very well downward, as the number cache hits increase as the frame data decreases.

So no, nothing weird here. Both RDNA3 and Lovelace scale pretty uniformly like Turing and RDNA1 did.

comments.text:
Used pricing? get real. Finding that price for a used 3080 2 years ago was nearly impossible anyway, and inflation has been a lot higher than normal over the past three years. You have to compare new pricing vs. new pricing, otherwise you're being very misleading. 

The 7800 XT naming is dumb. It's a 6700 XT successor, because it's using a mid-sized GPU, and its launching at a similar MSRP that the 6700 XT launched at. 500 USD today is equivalent to around 440 USD two and a half years ago, when the 6700 XT first launched at 480 USD, and the 7800 XT is about 43% faster than the 6700 XT.

It's nothing new for previous gen graphics cards to be heavily discounted in price before many of the next gen cards replace them, and for them to have equal or better performance per dollar at those prices, yet many people are arguing things like "the 7800 XT offers little to no improvement in value per dollar over the previous generation", as if AMD is supposed to give us a major improvement in value per dollar over CURRENT pricing for the already heavily discounted 6800 XT (and other various heavily discounted 6000 series cards). 

Do you need to like the price of the 7800 XT? No. It sucks that average incomes haven't kept pace with inflation, and you could argue that AMD does share some degree of blame for that, though certainly not most of the blame. 

If 500 is still too expensive for you, then that sucks, because the 7700 XT is not worth considering at current pricing (even though it is fairly competitive against Nvidia alternatives). The 6700 XT is currently a potentially very good option at 330 USD, but stock will probably mostly run out long before the next generation comes out, and the 7700 XT is simply too close in manufacturing cost to the 7800 XT for AMD to ever want to give us a genuinely good deal on them. AMD definitely left a big gap between the 7600 (which is itself still over-priced at most retailers), and the 7800 XT, basically forcing people to buy previous gen, or used cards, if they want a good value lower-mid-range or upper-low-end graphics card, and Nvidia has also basically done the same thing, by offering poor value for everything other than the RTX 4070 (and the 4090 is arguably a good value as well, at least as far as ultra high-end cards go, but it's simply not going to be worth buying for the vast majority of gamers).

comments.text:
And that's different, why? You could have gotten a 6800 XT back then for around the same price, what's the big deal? 

The 7800 XT naming is dumb. It's a 6700 XT successor, because it's using a mid-sized GPU, and its launching at a similar MSRP that the 6700 XT launched at. 500 USD today is equivalent to around 440 USD two and a half years ago, when the 6700 XT first launched at 480 USD, and the 7800 XT is about 43% faster than the 6700 XT.

It's nothing new for previous gen graphics cards to be heavily discounted in price before many of the next gen cards replace them, and for them to have equal or better performance per dollar at those prices, yet many people are arguing things like "the 7800 XT offers little to no improvement in value per dollar over the previous generation", as if AMD is supposed to give us a major improvement in value per dollar over CURRENT pricing for the already heavily discounted 6800 XT (and other various heavily discounted 6000 series cards). 

Do you need to like the price of the 7800 XT? No. It sucks that average incomes haven't kept pace with inflation, and you could argue that AMD does share some degree of blame for that, though certainly not most of the blame. 

If 500 is still too expensive for you, then that sucks, because the 7700 XT is not worth considering at current pricing (even though it is fairly competitive against Nvidia alternatives). The 6700 XT is currently a potentially very good option at 330 USD, but stock will probably mostly run out long before the next generation comes out, and the 7700 XT is simply too close in manufacturing cost to the 7800 XT for AMD to ever want to give us a genuinely good deal on them. AMD definitely left a big gap between the 7600 (which is itself still over-priced at most retailers), and the 7800 XT, basically forcing people to buy previous gen, or used cards, if they want a good value lower-mid-range or upper-low-end graphics card, and Nvidia has also basically done the same thing, by offering poor value for everything other than the RTX 4070 (and the 4090 is arguably a good value as well, at least as far as ultra high-end cards go, but it's simply not going to be worth buying for the vast majority of gamers).

comments.text:
The 7800 XT naming is dumb. It's a 6700 XT successor, because it's using a mid-sized GPU, and its launching at a similar MSRP that the 6700 XT launched at. 500 USD today is equivalent to around 440 USD two and a half years ago, when the 6700 XT first launched at 480 USD, and the 7800 XT is about 43% faster than the 6700 XT.

It's nothing new for previous gen graphics cards to be heavily discounted in price before many of the next gen cards replace them, and for them to have equal or better performance per dollar at those prices, yet many people are arguing things like "the 7800 XT offers little to no improvement in value per dollar over the previous generation", as if AMD is supposed to give us a major improvement in value per dollar over CURRENT pricing for the already heavily discounted 6800 XT (and other various heavily discounted 6000 series cards). 

Do you need to like the price of the 7800 XT? No. It sucks that average incomes haven't kept pace with inflation, and you could argue that AMD does share some degree of blame for that, though certainly not most of the blame. 

If 500 is still too expensive for you, then that sucks, because the 7700 XT is not worth considering at current pricing (even though it is fairly competitive against Nvidia alternatives). The 6700 XT is currently a potentially very good option at 330 USD, but stock will probably mostly run out long before the next generation comes out, and the 7700 XT is simply too close in manufacturing cost to the 7800 XT for AMD to ever want to give us a genuinely good deal on them. AMD definitely left a big gap between the 7600 (which is itself still over-priced at most retailers), and the 7800 XT, basically forcing people to buy previous gen, or used cards, if they want a good value lower-mid-range or upper-low-end graphics card, and Nvidia has also basically done the same thing, by offering poor value for everything other than the RTX 4070 (and the 4090 is arguably a good value as well, at least as far as ultra high-end cards go, but it's simply not going to be worth buying for the vast majority of gamers).

In Germany the VAT is 19% so the "correct" price for the 7800XT is ~550€ with today's exchange rate. In Denmark we have 25% VAT so the price would be ~583€. That you're seeing 6950XTs for just €620 in a few select stores is because the Euro has been gaining on the Dollar and they bought stock before that. So strike while you can, as that wont last.
